title: Linear Polarization of Light
short_intro: Linear polarization is a phenomenon of transverse waves where the electric field vector is restricted to vibrate along a single fixed plane containing the direction of propagation. It provides conclusive evidence of the transverse nature of light waves.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition of unpolarized and polarized light, Malus's Law, Brewster's Law, polarization by reflection and simple polarizers.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of electromagnetic waves, Jones calculus representation, double refraction in uniaxial crystals, quarter and half-wave plates, and optical activity.

prerequisites: Phase difference and superposition of simple harmonic motions

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Unpolarized and Polarized Light
bullets: Unpolarized light consists of rapidly and randomly changing electric field orientations perpendicular to the propagation vector with equal probability.
Linearly polarized light maintains a constant direction of the electric field vector throughout its propagation.
The intensity of unpolarized light passing through an ideal linear polarizer is reduced to exactly half its initial value.

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection and Brewster's Law
bullets: When unpolarized light strikes a dielectric boundary at a specific angle called the polarizing angle or Brewster's angle, the reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and the refracted (transmitted) ray are mutually perpendicular to each other.
The tangent of the polarizing angle is numerically equal to the relative refractive index of the medium.

concept_notes.heading: Malus's Law
bullets: Malus's Law governs the transmission of linearly polarized light through an analyzer.
The transmitted intensity varies directly as the square of the cosine of the angle between the transmission axes of the polarizer and the analyzer.
Maximum transmission occurs at zero degrees, and complete extinction occurs at ninety degrees.

concept_notes.heading: Double Refraction and Birefringence
bullets: Anisotropic crystals like calcite split an unpolarized incident ray into two refracted rays: the ordinary (O) ray and the extraordinary (E) ray.
The O-ray obeys ordinary laws of refraction and travels with the same speed in all directions within the crystal.
The E-ray does not obey ordinary Snell's law and its velocity varies with the direction of propagation inside the crystal.

derivations.title: Brewster's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Unpolarized light incident on a transparent dielectric boundary at polarizing angle ip
steps: Let i<sub>p</sub> be the angle of incidence (Brewster's angle) and r be the angle of refraction.
According to Snell's Law, n = \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin r}.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and refracted ray are perpendicular, so i_p + r = 90^{\circ}, which gives r = 90^{\circ} - i_p.
Substitute r into Snell's Law: n = \frac{\sin i_p}{\sin(90^{\circ} - i_p)} = \frac{\sin i_p}{\cos i_p} = \tan i_p.

derivations.title: Malus's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Plane polarized light of amplitude A incident on an analyzer with angle \theta between their transmission axes
steps: Let the electric field vector of the incident polarized light be represented by E = A \sin(\omega t).
The analyzer resolves this vector into two rectangular components: A \cos\theta parallel to the transmission axis and A \sin\theta perpendicular to it.
Only the component parallel to the transmission axis, A \cos\theta, is transmitted by the analyzer.
Since light intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude (I \propto A^{2}), the transmitted intensity I is given by I = I_0 \cos^2\theta, where I_0 \propto A^{2}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Malus's Law Verification Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of transmitted intensity I versus \cos^2\theta showing a straight line passing through the origin, or I versus \theta showing a symmetric cosine-squared wave curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms the quadratic dependence of transmitted light intensity on the cosine of the angle between polarizer transmission axes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual identification of intensity variations during polarizer rotation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization by Reflection Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Unpolarized ray incident on a glass slab at angle i_p, showing a reflected ray at angle i_p perpendicular to a refracted ray at angle r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates Brewster's condition where reflected light is completely plane-polarized with electric vectors perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Answering direct theoretical questions on angle between reflected and refracted rays.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nicol Prism Construction and Action
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A calcite crystal cut diagonally and cemented with Canada balsam, showing total internal reflection of the O-ray and transmission of the E-ray.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how a Nicol prism functions as an effective polarizer and analyzer by eliminating the ordinary ray.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions regarding optical components used to produce and analyze polarized light.

solved_numericals.question: Unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m^2 is incident on a polarizer. The transmitted light is then passed through an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle of 60 degrees with the polarizer axis. Find the final transmitted intensity.
solution_steps: Intensity after passing through the first polarizer: I_1 = \frac{1}{2} I_0 = \frac{1}{2} \times 32 = 16 \text{ W/m^2}.
Apply Malus's Law for the analyzer: I_2 = I_1 \cos^2\theta.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the polarizing angle for glass having a refractive index of 1.65. Also calculate the angle of refraction inside the glass.
solution_steps: Use the relation between angle of incidence and refraction at Brewster's angle: i_p + r = 90^{\circ}.

solved_numericals.question: A quarter-wave plate is designed for light of wavelength 589 nm. If the ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices for the crystal are 1.544 and 553 respectively (take \Delta n = 0.009), find the minimum thickness of the plate.
solution_steps: Formula for quarter-wave plate thickness: t = \frac{\lambda}{4(n_e - n_o)}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Ideal polarizers are assumed to absorb 100 percent of the perpendicular component and transmit 100 percent of the parallel component without internal scattering or absorption losses.
Brewster's law assumes isotropic dielectric media where magnetic permeability is approximately equal to that of free space (mu \approx mu_0).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Sound waves can be polarized just like light waves.
common_misconceptions.correct: Sound waves are longitudinal and cannot be polarized.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization is exclusively a property of transverse waves where vibrations occur perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The intensity of unpolarized light becomes zero after passing through a single ideal polarizer.
common_misconceptions.correct: The intensity becomes exactly half of the initial unpolarized intensity.
common_misconceptions.why: An ideal polarizer averages out the random transverse electric field components, transmitting half of the total incident intensity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are parallel.
common_misconceptions.correct: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are strictly perpendicular to each other.
common_misconceptions.why: The geometric condition derived from Snell's law and boundary conditions proves that i_p + r = 90 degrees.

quick_revision: Unpolarized light intensity drops to half through a single ideal polarizer: I = I_0 / 2.
Brewster's Law: n = \tan i_p, with reflected and refracted rays at 90 degrees.
A quarter-wave plate introduces a phase difference of \pi / 2 radians (path difference \lambda / 4).
A half-wave plate introduces a phase difference of \pi radians (path difference \lambda / 2).
